hook: A coffee chain times every car at its drive-through. Most cars wait 2 or 3 minutes, a few wait 12. If a manager averages a random sample of 40 cars, how far can that average land from the true mean of 4.2 minutes? The answer is a whole distribution, and it is much narrower and much more normal than the wait times themselves.

options: the values of a statistic over many random samples of the same size
the values in the whole population
the sample sizes a study could use
prereq.why: A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic, such as $\bar{x}$, across all possible samples of one size.

prereq.q: Heights are normal with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. What is the z-score of 182 cm?
prereq.why: $z = \frac{182 - 170}{8} = 1.5$: the value minus the mean, over the standard deviation.

prereq.q: Why does the 10% condition matter when sampling without replacement?
options: It keeps the observations close enough to independent for the standard deviation formula
It makes the sampling distribution normal
It removes bias from the sample
It makes the sample size large enough
prereq.why: Drawing a small share of a large population barely changes what is left, so the draws act independent.

figure.caption: Left: the skewed population of wait times. Middle and right: 5,000 simulated sample means for samples of 4 and of 40 cars. The center stays at 4.2 minutes, the spread shrinks like $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, and the shape becomes normal.

chain.effect: high and low values partly cancel, so means vary less than single values

chain.cause: On average over many samples, $\bar{x}$ hits the population mean
The variance of an average of $n$ independent values is $\frac{\sigma^2}{n}$
chain.effect: the standard deviation of $\bar{x}$ is $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ (when the sample is under 10% of the population)

chain.cause: Averaging many values smooths away skew
chain.effect: for $n \ge 30$ the sampling distribution is approximately normal (the central limit theorem); for a normal population it is normal at any $n$

chain.cause: With a normal model, center and spread
chain.effect: a z-score $\frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ gives probabilities about sample means

ideas: Spread: $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, valid when the sample is less than 10% of the population. Four times the sample size halves the spread.
Shape: normal if the population is normal; approximately normal if $n \ge 30$ (central limit theorem); otherwise it keeps some of the population's skew.
The central limit theorem is about the distribution of many sample means, not about the data in one sample.

misconception.wrong: With a large sample, the data become normal, so a skewed population gives a normal sample.
misconception.right: A large random sample looks like the population, skew and all. What becomes approximately normal is the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$, the pattern of the means over many samples.

summary: The sample mean $\bar{x}$ has a sampling distribution centered at $\mu$ with standard deviation $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ (10% condition). It is normal for a normal population and approximately normal for $n \ge 30$ by the central limit theorem. Standardize with $z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ to find probabilities about a sample mean.
